summary:
Lunar Sightline Planner is a browser-based lunar mission planning console that evaluates solar illumination & Earth visibility across potential landing sites & dates, enabling side-by-side comparison of up to four mission scenarios.

Users can select from curated historical & prospective landing sites—including Apollo, Chandrayaan-3, Chang’e 4, Shackleton, Malapert, Haworth, & Faustini—or enter custom lunar coordinates. Using DE421 ephemeris data, Earth libration, & LOLA-derived terrain horizons, the application calculates the Sun’s & Earth’s elevation & azimuth relative to the local horizon. It translates these calculations into operational visualizations, including sunrise & Earthrise countdowns, illumination & communication timelines, configurable feasibility screening, a 366-day temporal scan, permanent-shadow maps, & nearby-cell analysis for identifying alternative landing locations.

Lunar Sightline addresses the challenge of rapid lunar site evaluation. When launch delays, hardware constraints, or changing mission requirements necessitate a revised landing date or location, planners can immediately assess how those adjustments affect solar power availability, communication windows, & overall mission feasibility.

Designed to accommodate additional datasets, sites, & operational constraints, it provides an extensible foundation for evaluating the south pole’s rapidly changing environmental conditions & supporting better-informed lunar exploration decisions.
details:
Lunar Sightline Planner is a browser-based decision-support tool for evaluating sunlight and Earth visibility at potential lunar landing locations. These conditions matter especially near the lunar poles, where the Sun stays low above the horizon and small changes in terrain, location, or timing can determine whether a site receives sunlight or has an unobstructed view of Earth. The planner makes these relationships easier to examine together.

Users can select from 21 curated historical, mission-associated, and candidate locations or enter custom coordinates. They can choose a date and analysis period, step through time, compare up to four site-and-date scenarios, set screening thresholds, and scan a year for favorable periods. The calculations estimate the apparent positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the lunar surface, accounting for lunar motion and libration. A built-in analytic model supports the standard workflow, with an optional higher-accuracy SPICE calculation.

LOLA terrain elevation data informs local horizon profiles, which estimate whether ridges and crater rims block the Sun or Earth. All 21 curated locations have bundled profiles. Ten south-polar sites use local grids with resolutions ranging from 5 to 120 metres, while the other eleven use global terrain data at approximately 118 metres per pixel at the equator. Users can supply a terrain profile for a custom location; otherwise, custom coordinates use a spherical horizon. Some curated coordinates are approximate, so results at those locations should be interpreted accordingly.

The planner presents results through an interactive lunar globe, a local sky view, timelines, and event countdowns for the next sunrise or sunset and Earthrise or Earthset. It also reports periods of darkness and Earth-visibility gaps, and provides simplified solar-array incidence estimates for horizontal and vertical orientations. A shared time control links the visualizations so that a change in date or location can be followed across multiple views.

Polar map layers add regional context for average solar illumination, average Earth visibility, and permanent-shadow classification. The average illumination and visibility products summarize long-term conditions over approximately one lunar nutation cycle. The nearby-location scan uses downsampled map samples: its projected spacing is approximately 1.5 kilometres, 0.9 kilometres, and 0.3 kilometres across the three coverage bands. It is therefore intended for regional screening. Date-specific calculations are handled separately. Earth visibility is a geometric line-of-sight estimate.

The project is implemented in HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript, with Canvas 2D for interactive visualizations. A Node.js preprocessing step was used to derive terrain horizons from the large LOLA elevation grids. A standard desktop or laptop and modern browser are sufficient; no specialized hardware is required.

The project’s creative contribution lies in its connected workflow. Rather than presenting illumination, Earth visibility, terrain horizons, and schedules as separate outputs, the planner links them through a common time control and supports direct comparison of multiple locations and dates. The annual scan and nearby-location view extend this approach from a single prediction to exploration of alternatives. This integration helps users investigate how operational opportunities change when a landing location, date, or mission threshold changes.

Design considerations included the Moon’s lack of an atmosphere, low polar Sun angles, terrain obstruction, libration, variations in terrain resolution, and uncertainty in some site coordinates. The project also distinguishes long-term average map products from date-specific calculations and geometric Earth visibility from communications performance.

The intended impact is to make complex lunar environmental data easier to interpret for early mission comparison, education, and public engagement. The planner can help users identify dates and locations for further study and understand why polar exploration is operationally challenging.
